PL. 01 / 11THE BRIEF · THE FIELD0:10 – 0:32
01

One brief, one corpus, two brand modes: thirty-six decks and thirty-six explainers.

Every contender rendered the same product pitch — tokenized real-world assets — from the same read-only corpus, against the same three teaching goals: what the product is, what it is worth in this market, and how the basic mechanism works. The hardest constraint was the simplest: no invented numbers.

Each design tool then rendered it twice — once under a pinned house brand, once with no brand limits — against three messaging contracts. Six tools × two modes × three contracts = thirty-six tracks, each a deck and a timed explainer.

PL. 05 / 11WHAT THEY ALL DID1:10 – 1:24
05

Every tool rendered every slot in order — and every tool built the film engine itself.

Thirty of thirty decks and thirty of thirty explainers render every slot and scene, in order, claims verbatim, scene durations equal to the narration budget. The messaging contract as a transport works — a finding, not a given.

And no design skill has a timeline. All six wrote the clock, the scene seek and the progress bar themselves; the motion vocabulary came from the messaging layer. It is the clearest tooling gap in the run, and the reason no tool scores above seven for fit.

PL. 07 / 11THE DESIGN VERDICTS1:40 – 2:11
07

Brand mode produced the run’s only consensus. Free mode produced none at all.

Under the pinned brand, canvas-design takes first place on four of five rubrics and a rank sum of four out of a possible four — the only consensus in the bake-off. Across both modes it wins the run on nineteen, against 22.5 and 23.5 for the next two.

With no brand limits, every tool except one places first on at least one rubric and last or next-to-last on another. The rank sums span 9.5 to 16.5 with four tools inside two points. Reporting a free-mode winner would be manufacturing one.

SRC · bakeoff/JUDGING-design-claude.md §2 “The dispersion is the result”, §4
PL. 08 / 11WHAT THE REVIEWS FOUND · I2:11 – 2:26
08

Nine films of ten put their loudest frame somewhere other than their designated peak.

And one on-screen number is untraceable: a live particle count printed where a measurement belongs, in a readout whose value appears nowhere in the source corpus. Two reviews reach it independently; one calls it its highest-severity finding.

SRC · bakeoff/JUDGING-design-claude.md §3 findings 1–2 · reviews/design/by-messaging-rubrics.md
PL. 09 / 11WHAT THE REVIEWS FOUND · II2:26 – 2:44
09

The citation lines the brief made mandatory were set below the threshold of sight.

1.85:1 on the winner’s source line; 1.85:1 on another tool’s provenance line on every slide; 123 of 221 strings under the 4.5:1 floor in one deck. One reviewer calls a single token change here the highest-value fix in its whole review.

Internal contract vocabulary reached the client-facing surface in four of six tools. And the finishing pass bought the entire craft floor while closing not one composition finding — in either mode.

SRC · bakeoff/JUDGING-design-claude.md §3 findings 3, 5, 6, 8 · reviews/design/by-open-design-review.md
PL. 10 / 11WHAT IT COST2:44 – 3:08
10

The winning deck lost a fact, and reported that it had lost nothing.

One track dropped a line from a slide: the roll-cost figure that drives the drift number printed on that same slide. It is the only fact missing from any of the thirty decks, and the track’s own notes report that nothing was dropped.

Four rubrics ranked it first anyway. The fifth ranked it fourth — and the fifth is the only one that checked.
